title: When Team Members Face Personal Crisis, How Fast Do Their Challenges Become Yours as Well?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post argues that exceptional leaders respond to a team member's personal tragedy by co-owning the problem rather than merely offering help from a distance. It describes the practical forms this takes, such as finding doctors, arranging travel and care, and covering costs. Three stories anchor the claim: Barbara Beck of Cisco cooking a birthday meal for a terminally ill employee, Truett Cathy of Chick-fil-A quietly paying an operator's medical bills, and Herb Kelleher of Southwest rerouting a plane for an employee in crisis. The author adds that this behavior only works when the team knows the leader wants to hear about trouble, so word reaches the leader early. The closing move is organizational: when those at the top model this, others receive permission to do likewise and it becomes the norm.
points: Exceptional leaders go beyond asking how they can help and begin to share ownership of the crisis itself, handling concrete logistics.
The payoff for co-owning a crisis is trust, retention in hard times, and discretionary effort that compensation cannot purchase.
The Beck, Cathy and Kelleher stories show a common pattern of picking up part of the burden personally instead of delegating to a program or note.
Leaders only learn of crises early if the team knows they genuinely want to know.
Because crises are constant in large organizations, caring must be modeled from the top so many leaders feel permitted to act.
quotes: They don’t just inquire about how they can help and stay abreast of the issues. They subtly begin to own the problem alongside the team member in crisis.

This is how the best leaders express the compassion they feel and the loyalty they hope is reciprocal. Not many leaders express their caring this way, but those who do are rewarded with something compensation can’t buy: teams that trust them without reservation, team members who stay through hard times, and people who go above and beyond because they know their commitment will be returned when they need it most.
She didn’t ask from a distance what she could do. She picked up part of the burden and carried it herself.
Cathy didn’t send a note or refer the operator to an assistance program. Instead, he covered the bills himself.

Of course, co-owning a crisis starts with learning about who needs support, and that only happens when everyone on the team knows the leader genuinely wants to know. When the team knows that the leader doesn’t want any tragedy or personal crisis to go unattended, word reaches the leader long before it would travel through normal channels.

In large organizations, someone is almost always in crisis, so carrying such burdens takes an army of exceptionally caring leaders, not just one. That only happens when those at the top set the example.
